name: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7
route: Applied to the skin in serums and creams
status: Cosmetic ingredient; not an FDA-approved drug
mechanism: Proposed to dampen inflammation signals such as interleukin-6 so skin shows less age and sun damage; human proof is lacking

article.summary: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is a skincare peptide marketed to calm inflammation and smooth lines, usually paired with palmitoyl tripeptide-1. Human evidence for it alone is lacking.
article.takeaway: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 (Pal-GQPR) is a four-amino-acid peptide with a fatty acid attached, usually sold as a pair with [palmitoyl tripeptide-1](/peptides/palmitoyl-tripeptide-1) under the name Matrixyl 3000. It is proposed to reduce interleukin-6, an inflammatory signal that builds up in sun-aged skin, though human proof of that effect was not found. A 12-week eye-cream study that included both peptides reported better hydration, elasticity and collagen density, but the cream held other actives, so the peptides cannot be credited alone.[^1] In a 2026 study of three volunteers, Pal-GQPR stayed in the outermost skin barrier.[^2] **Evidence is limited.**
glance: Serums and eye creams, usually once or twice daily

blocks.text: Sun exposure and aging keep skin in a low-level inflammatory state, with signals such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) that can promote collagen breakdown. Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is proposed to turn that signal down, which in theory protects collagen. This mechanism is described by manufacturers; the verified studies here did not measure it in people.

The palmitoyl group, a fatty acid, is added to help the peptide stay in and cross the skin's oily outer barrier. It is one of four cosmetic peptide types described in a 2009 review, the signal peptides.[^3]

rows: A cream with palmitoyl tripeptide-1, palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7, a fermentation filtrate and N-acetylneuraminic acid raised hydration 28%, elasticity 19% and collagen density 55% on instruments; the abstract describes no comparison group and the ingredients cannot be separated[^1]
Three volunteers, serum with both peptides (2026)
Both peptides were found through the stratum corneum, the outer dead-cell layer, with signal falling steeply with depth and apparently sitting outside the cells; deeper layers were not assessed[^2]
Human trials of the peptide alone

blocks.text: A systematic review of over-the-counter anti-aging ingredients found that good supporting data are often missing.[^4]

It appears in anti-aging serums and eye creams, mostly as part of the Matrixyl 3000 pair. Products are applied once or twice a day, and any change would take weeks, as in the 12-week study.[^1] Labels seldom state how much active peptide is present.

The 2024 study described a high safety profile for the finished eye cream, but peptide-specific safety data are scarce.[^1] Irritation or allergy to other ingredients in the formula is the usual risk.
Cosmetics do not need FDA approval before sale, and a product that claims to change how skin works can be treated as a drug.[^5]

Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is a popular but poorly documented ingredient. The anti-inflammatory idea is plausible, yet the human data blend it with other actives, and skin-layer data suggest it may stay near the surface.

evidence.label: Very limited: only combination-product data
evidence.text: Human data come from multi-ingredient creams, and a skin-layer study suggests the peptide stays near the surface.[^1][^2] Reviews note that supporting data for anti-aging cosmetic ingredients are often lacking.[^4]

faq.q: Is Matrixyl 3000 the same as palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7?
faq.a: Matrixyl 3000 is a branded blend of two peptides, palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7.[^2]

faq.q: Does it reduce inflammation in the skin?
faq.a: That is the proposed mechanism, but the studies cited here did not measure inflammation markers in people.[^1]
The only skin-layer data found came from three volunteers and covered the outermost layer, where the signal fell with depth.[^2]
